text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
--Novo Nordisk's German unit is bucking a stagnant trend on the German pharmaceutical market and expects over 10 percent growth for the eighth consecutive year in 1997.

--The amicable separation between Danish hi-fi and tv maker Bang & Olufsen and Dutch electronics giant Philips --whereby B&O is to buy back Philips' 25 percent stake -- is in contrast to Philips' relations with Germany's Grundig . Philips is disputing Grundig losses of $364 million and plans to reduce its holding so that it is no longer responsible for all Grundig's losses. Grundig's troubles could allow B&O to pick up market share in Germany.
--U.S. pork producers plan to increase their market share, particulalry in Asia. This will come largely at the expense of Danish pork exporters who cannot compete on price.
--The Danish construction industry accepts criticism of poor quality and its leaders are to meet housing minister Ole Loevig Simonsen for talks on how to raise standards.

--The dispute over use of the Dankort debit card for internet shopping continues. Suppliers and the consumer council believe that the purchaser should pay the extra costs of processing card purchases but banks insist that the supplier pay.

--The Danish stock market is booming. It reached a total value of 620 million crowns on Monday and has gained 120 million since the beginning of the year. In the same period the KFX and all-share indices had risen by about 24 percent.
--Brondby football club's oversubscribed share offering shows that soccer stocks are not only for fans but are attracting the interest of professional investors.

--U.S. investment group Franklin Research and Development, which also co-ordinates the Coalition for Corporate Withdrawal from Burma, is pressuring Denmark's East Asiatic Company to halt its sales of herbicide to Burma.
--Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft has given local authorities permission to raise their taxes to finance hospital care and psychiatric services.
